newsitem.title: UK: Europe's investors in Iran oil relaxed as row brews.
newsitem.headline: Europe's investors in Iran oil relaxed as row brews.

text.p: European oil companies said on Friday they would not be deterred from investments in Iran despite a new crisis in relations between the European Union and Tehran.

France's Total, the only European oil company spending heavily in Iran, said it would continue with its controversial project to develop the Sirri oil and gas fields. The project dates back to July 1995.
"What is sure is that today it is not forbidden to invest in Iran," a Total spokesman said.

A German court ruling on Thursday, accusing Tehran of ordering the murder of dissidents in Berlin, sparked an international diplomatic row with Germany, Sweden and Australia recalling their ambassadors from Iran and the EU inviting other members to join the action.
Anglo-Dutch oil giant Shell said on Friday it would continue to talk to Iran about developing Iran's massive gas reserves despite the worsening relations between the European Union and Tehran.

Shell, which has been leading a consortium in talks with the National Iranian Oil Company (NIOC) over second phase development of the huge South Pars gas field, said it saw no reason to break off the dialogue.

"We continue to talk to Iran about South Pars, that's as far as it goes... Should anything come to fruition we would hope that the situation had been sorted out before then between governments," a Shell spokesman said.

The lure of Iran's gas reserves -- the world's second largest after Russia at 23 trillion cubic meters -- drew a crowd of international oil executives to a conference in Iran in February despite the threat of U.S. trade sanctions.

The Iran-Libya Sanctions Act sponsored by Senator Alfonse D'Amato and signed by U.S. President Bill Clinton last year, gives the president discretionary power to punish non-U.S. firms that invest $40 million or more a year in either of the two countries' oil and gas sectors.
But most European oil companies have ignored the U.S. threat. In January, Total chairman Thierry Desmarest confirmed the company was also interested in developing South Pars.

The enormous offshore field, which stretches over 3,700 square km (1,430 square miles) of Iranian territory, will not be producing before 1999 but NIOC is expected to award a $1 billion-plus contract to an international consortium later this year for the second phase.

Iran, a member of the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) and the world's third biggest oil exporter after Saudi Arabia and Norway, is keen to fulfil its huge potential as a gas producer.

South Pars, which holds around 40 percent of the Islamic Republic's gas reserves, is critical to its plans to keep pace with growing local demand and realise export projects to Pakistan, India and Europe.
BG plc formerly British Gas, which sent executives to the Iranian conference in February, said it was keeping an eye on events.
"We don't have any activities in Iran at the moment but we will be keeping the situation under review," said a BG spokesman.
British Petroleum said recently it had no immediate plans to invest in Iran.
